post1.text:
Most leaders think scaling a company is an operational problem. It is not. It is a leadership problem that shows up as an operational problem.

When companies push past $50M, the leadership behaviors that got them there become the ceiling holding them back. Recent research on executive development patterns at high-growth firms confirms this: the organizational principles that separate scaling winners from stalled companies almost always trace back to how the person at the top makes decisions, delegates authority, and tolerates discomfort.

Three things leaders at this stage consistently get wrong:

1. They optimize for loyalty over capability when building their senior team.
2. They treat culture as a communication problem rather than a structural one.
3. They confuse being busy with leading well.

Scaling past $100M is not about working harder or hiring more people. It is about becoming a fundamentally different kind of leader before the business demands it of you.

What leadership behavior are you holding onto that your company has already outgrown?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Yahoo Finance highlights how Scale Smart Leaders and Jeff Bezos point to strikingly similar organizational principles when it comes to developing executives inside growing companies.

What stood out to us at Autobahn: this is not a coincidence. The best-run scaling companies build leadership development into the structure of the organization, not as a perk or an annual offsite, but as a repeating system.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this matters more than most leaders realize. You cannot scale a company faster than you scale the people leading it. If your executive bench is not growing in capability, your revenue ceiling is closer than your forecast suggests.

Read the full piece and think about where your leadership pipeline actually stands: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMioAFBVV95cUxQYkgxSi16MG9YQVJ6N1FTNS1JS2xhNVBndFdpMEFHTVhqRjJiWDVONWFuV29pSFdRMDFwRlVOUGlUM0s0RUdGU2ZHbVdGdzFicWdnTjRGd29tY1VzZFJMX3pUSGEtVXZ4LU5Oa1RHTXczUkhqYzFaR19JMDBfY2lQb0FWUHVFZzlsQXpDZThBVi1CaFZ5VjVKSkQwUDZSV05Q

post3.text:
The Yahoo Finance piece on executive development principles got our attention, because it points directly at something Katherine Slain addresses in Chapter 1 of our upcoming book.

The chapter is called "Lead Like Lives Depend On It," and the title is intentional. Katherine's premise is not that leadership is dramatic. It is that the stakes at the $50M to $500M stage are higher than most leaders treat them, and the gap between good leadership and great leadership is exactly where scaling stalls.

One thing Katherine surfaces early: the leaders who scale successfully are not the ones who have all the answers. They are the ones who have built the right relationship with uncertainty at the top.

That distinction sounds small. The business results it produces are not.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

The executives who figure this out early build organizations that compound. The ones who do not spend years adding revenue while quietly building a ceiling above themselves. Here is what the research and the practitioners are telling us right now.

post1.text:
Most business owners think about their exit too late. By the time you are ready to sell, the window to maximize your multiple has already closed.

Here is what mid-market leaders consistently get wrong: they confuse a liquidity event with an exit strategy. One is a transaction. The other is a years-long process that begins long before any buyer shows up.

J.P. Morgan's private banking team has outlined this distinction clearly, noting that the best exits are engineered, not stumbled into. That tracks with what we see at $50M to $500M companies every day.

Three things that actually move your valuation multiple upward before you go to market:

1. Demonstrable, recurring revenue with low customer concentration
2. A management team that can run the business without you
3. Clean financials with at least three years of consistent EBITDA growth

Owners who build these things intentionally command a premium. Those who do not, leave money on the table.

What is the one thing in your business that a buyer would flag as a risk on day one?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Silicon Valley Bank on exit strategies raises a point that does not get enough attention: knowing when NOT to sell is just as important as knowing when to pull the trigger.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, timing is only part of the equation. The bigger issue is readiness. A company that enters a sale process underprepared will either lose the deal, accept a lower multiple, or both.

At Autobahn, we work with leadership teams to close the gap between where a business is today and where it needs to be to attract the right buyer at the right price. That work takes time, and it has to start before a banker is ever engaged.

If you are thinking about an exit in the next two to five years, the work starts now.

Read the SVB piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMinwFBVV95cUxQeXI2ZzYxYnJkdGhyZ1FlaVBlWXQ1RjB4ZnhCRWtFVEpBZ0FPZnB4amFmV2xxVmxJbXRMR0dfeHlmWkw2V0syR3pfdGdMaGJvMDVQQ1hJZUgwaU1wcnRFVkU0aExWQ01yQUJFQTd3Z0NrZG9sR3Q3XzQ5cF9IZEJuWDdsNmZ5dUJjVjZ3NEZqQ2preC1henhFRnV6MWtXRWc

post3.text:
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce recently published a solid primer on building a business exit strategy. It covers the fundamentals well. But for companies operating at $50M and above, the fundamentals are just the entry fee.

Chapter 2 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled "Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit." Written by Paul Belair and George Hohman, it goes deeper than most exit planning conversations dare to go.

One thing the chapter makes clear: your multiple is not set by the market. It is set by the decisions you make two to four years before you ever sit across from a buyer. There is a specific set of levers that high-performing mid-market companies pull to move that number, and most owners have never been shown what those levers are.

Rock Your Business -- available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because the strategy was wrong, but because leadership never agreed on what execution actually looks like.

Forbes recently explored why leadership teams consistently break down at the execution stage. The core problem is not lack of effort. It is lack of shared definition. Everyone leaves the planning meeting believing something slightly different about what success means and who owns what.

Here is what scaling companies need to hear:

1. Strategy without an owner is a wish. Every initiative needs a single accountable person, not a committee.

2. Quarterly check-ins are too slow. At the $50M to $500M stage, you need monthly rhythm at minimum to course-correct before drift becomes damage.

3. The gap between planning and execution widens every time leadership communicates the what without the why. Context is not optional.

Companies that scale well treat execution as a discipline, not an afterthought to the annual offsite.

So here is the question worth sitting with: Does your leadership team have a shared, written definition of what successful execution looks like this quarter?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Harvard Business School Online tackled one of the most persistent problems in growing companies: getting employees to actually buy into strategic initiatives.

The insight is real, but here is what the article does not say loudly enough. At the $50M to $500M stage, buy-in is not a culture problem. It is a communication architecture problem. Leaders assume that because they announced the strategy, people understand it. Those are not the same thing.

Scaling companies need repeatable systems for translating strategy into team-level priorities, not just town halls and slide decks.

If your people are not moving in the direction you planned, the question to ask is not why they are resistant. Ask whether they ever had a clear line of sight from their daily work to the company goal.

Read the full piece here and then ask yourself what your execution architecture actually looks like: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiXEFVX3lxTE10NVhQek5OWEJXOHdQLW1iZFF5dWN0Vy1TS0VJMzJUYmQ1ZWRVUzZLWk50QTdNbHpEd3JtS2ZfbFFZSWR6MTNJMnZraWMzUVNrUVl6LTE5T2FCMVhW?oc=5

post3.text:
The strategy execution problem is not new. But the lessons that stick tend to come from unexpected places.

Chapter 3 of our upcoming book Rock Your Business, titled What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes, is written by Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall. It draws on real operational experience across wildly different industries to surface a truth that most planning frameworks miss: the conditions that make a strategy executable are often decided long before the strategy is ever written.

Most leadership teams focus on what the plan says. Rafa and Jim focus on what the organization can actually absorb and sustain. That distinction changes everything about how you build your roadmap from $50M toward $500M.

The details of their framework are worth the read on their own.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most $50M+ companies don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. A habit is what your team does because it worked before. A strategy is a deliberate system built to win specific customers, repeatedly, at scale.

McKinsey recently surfaced data that reframes the stakes: B2B companies that fail to build sustainable growth engines aren't just leaving money on the table. They're falling behind a rising survival threshold that keeps moving up.

Here's what that means in practice for scaling companies:

1. Referrals and relationships alone will not get you to $500M. They got you to $50M. That's not the same road.

2. Without a defined Ideal Customer Profile tied to a repeatable motion, every new rep you hire is winging it at your expense.

3. Revenue growth without sales infrastructure creates fragility, not scale.

The companies winning right now didn't get lucky. They got intentional.

What does your sales strategy actually prescribe that your team couldn't figure out on their own?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Bain lays out what separates B2B growth leaders from the rest: a repeatable, systematic approach to capturing new customers rather than relying on one-off wins and warm introductions.

This matters enormously for companies in the $50M to $500M range. At that stage, you can no longer afford a sales team where every rep has their own playbook. What got you here was hustle. What gets you there is infrastructure.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly. Leadership assumes they have a sales strategy because they have a sales team. Those are not the same thing.

If your growth depends on who shows up to work that day rather than the system they're working, that's the problem worth solving first.

Read the Bain piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiuwFBVV95cUxNTnFuY29VYUwzZ2FBUUstT3NwOGJncXBFSm03ajFydXhEMUxzOVZRaXE0VndTOEtzX2ZfQUtySjJFX1F3ek1aTXRreFFJLUdyOWY1bWZ3RFZiTGNTNFlIVmtHVURtOW55bzBsVFREVXJudUE4TmhqZUVOSFZLUE5YNE1weU5NV0Rla3hxMW1oZDhTd3ZvR1lUQm9xRm04cFVQNUZBQ19lZnBxMnFBZXJjQVNNV2RWMWJsMmJV?oc=5

post3.text:
New research showing B2B companies must now meet a rising survival threshold to grow isn't surprising to Deb and Brandon, co-authors of Chapter 4 in our upcoming book.

The chapter is called "Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation." That title is not a metaphor. It's math.

Deb and Brandon work with scaling companies every day, and the pattern is consistent: leadership treats sales activity as a proxy for sales strategy. Busy pipelines. Active reps. Optimistic forecasts. And still, growth stalls somewhere between $50M and $100M with no one sure why.

Chapter 4 identifies exactly where the gap lives and gives leadership a clear way to see it before it costs another quarter.

The insight that tends to land hardest? Most companies already have the ingredients for a real sales strategy. They just haven't assembled them deliberately.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: If your company grew to $50M on relationships, referrals, and relentless hustle, congratulations. Now comes the harder question: what exactly happens when that stops being enough? The difference between companies that scale past $100M and those that plateau isn't effort. It's whether leadership has built a sales strategy that works independent of any single person in the room.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is not your color palette. Your brand is what people feel when they are not looking at any of those things.

Most $50M+ companies treat marketing like a production line. Push out content, run ads, measure clicks. But attention has become scarce, and the businesses winning right now are the ones building something people actually remember. Research from brand strategists tracking AI-era consumer behavior confirms it: emotional resonance outperforms volume every time.

Three things scaling companies get wrong about their brand:

1. They market to everyone, which means they reach no one with any real conviction.
2. They confuse activity with strategy. Posting more is not a plan.
3. They let their brand drift as they grow, so customers at $200M cannot describe what made the company great at $50M.

Your brand should have a point of view strong enough to repel the wrong customers and attract the right ones.

What does your company stand for that a competitor could not credibly copy tomorrow?

#BrandStrategy #ScalingBusiness #MarketingLeadership

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive on Ulta's CMO caught our attention, and not just because it's about a recognizable consumer brand.

The core argument is simple: brand building and performance marketing are not opposing forces. The companies that treat them as separate budgets with separate goals end up with neither a strong brand nor reliable growth.

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, this tension shows up constantly. Leadership chases short-term revenue metrics while the brand quietly loses coherence. By the time someone notices, re-establishing brand identity costs far more than maintaining it would have.

The lesson: your brand strategy and your channel strategy need to be built in the same room, by the same people, toward the same goals.

Read the full piece and think about where those two conversations are happening in your organization.

post3.text:
What does your marketing smell like?

That is not a trick question. It is the opening challenge of Chapter 5 in our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond.

Chapter 5 authors Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West make the case that by the time a company hits $50M, its brand has usually developed an identity by accident rather than by design. Leadership has been too focused on revenue to notice.

The chapter gives scaling companies a framework for diagnosing what their brand is actually communicating versus what leadership thinks it is communicating. That gap is almost always bigger than expected, and it is almost always costing money.

If your marketing feels like it is working hard without working together, this chapter will tell you why.

By $50M, your marketing has usually accumulated years of inconsistent messaging, misaligned channels, and assumptions nobody has tested. post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost problem disguised as ambition.

SHRM recently reported that the most effective hiring organizations in 2026 are moving away from volume-based recruiting and toward precision targeting. They are filling fewer roles, faster, with higher retention rates. That is not a coincidence.

Here is what mid-market leaders scaling past $50M need to understand:

1. Your org chart from last year is already wrong. Growth exposes structural gaps that more headcount cannot fix. You need to redesign roles before you recruit into them.

2. Speed-to-productivity matters more than speed-to-hire. A 90-day onboarding ramp that actually works is worth more than cutting your time-to-fill by two weeks.

3. Talent strategy should be set at the leadership table, not delegated entirely to HR. The companies scaling well treat people decisions with the same rigor they apply to capital allocation.

If you are adding headcount without a clear talent architecture underneath it, what exactly are you building toward?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM titled 'Precision Over Scale: The New Rules of Hiring in 2026' makes a point that every scaling company should hear: the era of broad, high-volume recruiting is giving way to something sharper and more intentional.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this shift is not optional. At that stage, one bad hire at the director level or above can stall a quarter. One unfilled role in the wrong seat can break a growth initiative entirely.

Precision hiring means knowing exactly what a role needs to produce before you post it. It means evaluating talent against your next stage of growth, not your current one.

If your recruiting process still looks the same as it did when you were half your current size, it is time to revisit it.

Read the full SHRM piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMioAFBVV95cUxPRFVYR0VscXJpMmVqV2dwazJDTkstVDJTNG9uTlZlWHJPVkFqQ0MzZTRQSUYwUDZweWw2dE52THZKSnhBTzQtb1g5UUYzbmJTbjFJcXlVYno2ZzU4aE0yNVRwN2RIN05xTWJVWnZQejVyY2xRNmJ2SF83QmVHel9GYmdWTEdEMWZLMVk5OThMNTF0TmdKR1F4bG84cnZRZ0FU?oc=5

post3.text:
The conversation around precision hiring and talent architecture is exactly what Chapter 6 of our upcoming book addresses head-on.

In 'Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond,' Chapter 6 is called The Talent Engine. It was written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West, three practitioners who have worked inside scaling companies and seen what breaks first when growth outpaces the people strategy holding it together.

One thing the chapter makes clear: most mid-market companies do not have a hiring problem. They have a talent architecture problem. The fix does not start with a job posting. It starts somewhere most leaders overlook entirely.

We will leave it there for now.

post1.text:
More metrics will not save your business. They will bury it.

Most leadership teams at the $50M to $500M stage fall into the same trap: they add KPIs every quarter and remove none. The dashboard grows. Clarity shrinks. Decisions slow down.

A recent analysis from Business.com on KPI tracking tools revealed something worth sitting with: the problem most companies have is not a shortage of data. It is a shortage of discipline around which data actually drives decisions.

Three things scaling companies get wrong with metrics:

1. They track activity instead of outcomes. Busy numbers feel productive. They rarely are.

2. They confuse reporting with accountability. A number on a slide is not the same as an owner responsible for moving it.

3. They build dashboards for investors, not operators. If your frontline leaders cannot act on a metric by Friday, it has no business being in your weekly review.

The best-run companies we work with track fewer things, faster, with clearer owners.

What is one metric your team tracks that nobody has acted on in the last 90 days?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business.com rounded up 14 tools companies can use to track KPIs more effectively. It is a solid list. But here is what the article does not address: for scaling companies, the tool is rarely the problem.

At Autobahn, we work with businesses moving from $50M to $500M. At that stage, leadership teams typically have access to plenty of tracking software. What they lack is agreement on which five to ten numbers actually matter to the business right now, and who owns each one.

Adding a better tool to a bloated metrics system gives you faster access to the wrong information.

Before evaluating another platform, audit what you are already measuring and cut anything without a clear owner and a clear consequence.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
The business world keeps publishing lists of metrics to track. 14 tools. 31 social KPIs. 33 real estate measures. The lists keep getting longer.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business pushes back on all of it.

Titled 'Death by KPIs,' and authored by Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, this chapter tackles one of the most common and costly problems we see in scaling companies: leadership teams drowning in data while starving for direction.

One insight the authors surface early: there is a direct correlation between the number of KPIs a company tracks and the number of people who feel accountable for none of them. Measurement without ownership is just noise.

If your team spends more time building reports than acting on them, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business -- available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most companies are using AI wrong, and the productivity numbers prove it.

A new report found that nine out of ten executives say AI has not meaningfully improved productivity in their organizations. That is not a technology problem. That is a strategy problem.

Here is what mid-market leaders scaling past $50M need to understand:

1. AI does not create leverage by replacing tasks. It creates leverage by multiplying the output of your highest-value people. If you are deploying it at the bottom of your org chart first, you are optimizing in the wrong direction.

2. The companies seeing real gains are treating AI as a third layer of thinking, not a shortcut. They build it into decision workflows, not just content creation.

3. Cutting headcount before proving AI-generated output quality is a bet most scaling companies cannot afford to lose. Speed of growth forgives very little.

The question is not whether your team is using AI. The question is whether your leadership team has decided what AI is actually for.

What is the one decision in your business that AI could genuinely improve right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Bloomberg compiled AI productivity tactics from twelve CEOs and senior leaders, and the patterns are worth paying attention to.

The executives who are winning with AI are not the ones with the biggest budgets or the most tools. They are the ones who made deliberate choices about where their own time was leaking and built AI into those specific gaps.

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, that intentionality is everything. At that stage, the CEO's time is not just valuable, it is structural. How you spend it shapes the entire organization's capacity to grow.

If you are leading a scaling business and AI still feels like an experiment rather than an operating advantage, this article is a useful gut check.

Nine out of ten executives say AI has not moved the needle on productivity. That number does not surprise Hudson Shank or Jonathan Slain.

In Chapter 8 of Rock Your Business, titled The Third Monitor Theory, Hudson and Jonathan make a case that most leaders are not suffering from a lack of AI tools. They are suffering from a lack of a framework for where AI actually belongs in the work of running and scaling a business.

The Third Monitor Theory is not about adding a screen to your desk. It is about creating a distinct layer in how your leadership team processes information, makes decisions, and compounds output over time.

If AI feels like noise right now, this chapter will help you find the signal.

post1.text:
Imposter syndrome is not a weakness to fix. It is a signal that you are operating at the edge of your capability, which is exactly where growth happens.

Fast Company recently made the case that leaders who lean into that discomfort, rather than suppress it, actually perform better over time. That tracks with what we see at the $50M to $500M stage.

Here is what scaling leaders need to understand:

1. The feeling does not go away when you get bigger. Revenue milestones do not reset your psychology. Leaders who scale past $100M still report the same internal doubts they had at $10M.

2. Suppressing it costs more than admitting it. Leaders who hide doubt from their teams create cultures where nobody admits problems early. That is how small fires become crises.

3. The goal is not confidence. It is clarity. Knowing your gaps, naming them, and building around them is a leadership skill, not a character flaw.

The leaders who struggle most at scale are often not the least capable. They are the ones who confuse self-doubt with incompetence.

When did you last treat doubt as useful information instead of something to push through?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes highlighted something worth pausing on: women are dominating the travel industry in leadership roles, yet imposter syndrome remains widespread among them.

The achievement does not cancel the doubt. That is the part most leadership development programs miss entirely.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders scaling companies from $50M to $500M and beyond. At that stage, the external results look strong. Revenue is up. Teams are growing. The brand is gaining ground. But internally, many leaders are running on a quiet fear that they do not quite belong in the room they built.

That gap between outer success and inner narrative is not a personal problem. It is a scaling problem. Left unaddressed, it shapes decisions, stifles delegation, and limits how far a company can actually go.

post3.text:
What if the leaders most likely to struggle at scale are not the least qualified, but the ones most convinced they should not be struggling?

Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business, titled How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It, takes that question seriously. Written by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo, the chapter digs into the psychology of imposter syndrome at the leadership level, specifically for executives navigating the $50M to $500M growth window.

One of the sharpest insights in the chapter is that imposter syndrome at scale is not about self-esteem. It is about identity. The person who built a $50M company has to become someone different to lead a $500M one, and that transition carries real psychological weight.

That tension is worth understanding before it costs you your next stage of growth.

post1.text:
Most founders treat life planning like a retirement project. That is exactly why so many of them end up miserable after they hit their number.

Research consistently shows that a significant majority of founders who exit their businesses report deep regret within the first year. Not because the deal was bad. Because they never defined what they were building toward beyond the business itself.

Here is what leaders scaling past $50M need to understand:

1. Your business is a vehicle, not a destination. If you cannot articulate where the vehicle is supposed to take you, you will keep driving in circles at higher speeds.

2. Work-life design is not a balance problem. It is a clarity problem. The founders who thrive are the ones who get specific about what a good life actually looks like for them before the pressure of scale makes every day reactive.

3. Wealth without intention creates its own chaos. Financial planning and life planning are not the same conversation, and conflating them is a costly mistake.

So here is the question worth sitting with: If you hit your revenue target tomorrow, would you know what to do next?

#BusinessGrowth #Entrepreneurship #LeadershipDevelopment

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur caught our attention: 75% of founders regret selling their business within a year of the transaction.

The reason is almost never the deal terms. It is that founders spend years optimizing for the exit and zero time designing what comes after it.

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M and beyond, this is not just an exit planning issue. It is a leadership issue happening right now. When a founder cannot answer what success looks like outside the business, every major decision inside the business gets distorted.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders to close that gap before it becomes a crisis. The time to think about life design is during the scale, not after the sale.

Read the full article here and ask yourself whether your current growth plan has a human being at the center of it.

post3.text:
When three out of four founders regret selling their business within a year, that is not a financial planning failure. That is a life planning failure.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, tackles this directly. Authored by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain, the chapter challenges scaling leaders to stop treating personal vision as something that gets figured out after the business is built.

One insight from the chapter that reframes everything: the leaders who sustain success at $500M and beyond are almost always the ones who designed a life worth living before they needed to. The business becomes sharper, not softer, when the person running it has real clarity about what it is for.

There is a framework inside this chapter that most consultants will never bring up with you. We think it is some of the most important work in the book.
